content.text:
I found several credible performance opportunities. The strongest is not rendering—it’s repeated full-world work in the rules layer.

1. Highest potential: AI occupancy checks

[aiChaseSystem.js:304]( /home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/systems/aiChaseSystem.js:304 ) scans every `Position` entity whenever an AI checks whether a candidate tile is traversable:

```js
for (const [id, pos] of world.query(Position)) {
```

This happens inside per-monster movement decisions and sometimes multiple times per monster. The repo already has a spatial index, so this can become a cell lookup. That changes the scaling from roughly `monsters × world entities` to `monsters × nearby occupants`.

The trap check at [aiChaseSystem.js:143]( /home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/systems/aiChaseSystem.js:143 ) has the same issue: it scans every `Position, Trap` entity for each candidate tile.

2. High potential: material reactions

[materialReactionSystem.js:503]( /home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/systems/materialReactionSystem.js:503 ) scans every positioned entity every tick, even when no entity has a relevant burning/status source.

For active status sources, ground reactions then scan every `Position, ItemInfo` entity again at [materialReactionSystem.js:428]( /home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/systems/materialReactionSystem.js:428 ).

Measured cost:

- Normal live scenario: ~0.44–0.53 ms/tick.
- 256-actor scenario: ~3.3 ms/tick.
- 600-combat-pair scenario: ~4.15 ms/tick.

This is a good candidate for event-driven status-source tracking or indexed ground-item lookup.

3. Medium/high potential: item proc tick duplication

[itemProcTickSystem.js:20]( /home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/systems/itemProcTickSystem.js:20 ) evaluates every carried item, then evaluates equipped items again under a second trigger kind. Each evaluation rebuilds/traverses proc topology and resolves derived stats.

It accounts for about 10.3–10.6% of normal live simulation time. Likely improvements:

- cache compiled proc-node lists;
- resolve actor source stats once per tick;
- avoid repeated topology traversal;
- only evaluate equipped items twice if the two trigger semantics truly differ.

The recorded Entire checkpoint confirms this system was introduced as part of the generic carried/equipped proc topology, so this area should be optimized carefully without collapsing those semantics.

4. Rendering is significant but not the first target

The benchmark reports:

- `buildWorldView` with 3,500 entities: ~13.9 ms/call.

That is potentially close to a 60 FPS frame budget by itself, but the view already limits entity collection spatially around the player. The biggest likely render improvement would be caching static projections and avoiding repeated full ECS queries for unchanged data—not a small canvas drawing tweak.

5. Scenario-specific cliffs

The profiling tools found larger but narrower bottlenecks:

- `movementSystem`: ~23 ms/tick with 2,000 actors.
- `combatSystem`: ~110 ms/tick with 600 simultaneous attacks.

Those are clearly scalable problems for stress tests, but less likely to affect ordinary gameplay than the AI/material full scans.

One benchmark issue also surfaced: `deno task bench` fails during `headless.bench.mjs` dungeon generation because `getMonstersByTier(tier)` returns `undefined` in `pickMonster`. The independent system benchmarks still ran, but the overall benchmark task is not currently clean.

My recommended optimization order:

1. Replace AI tile occupancy scans with spatial-cell queries.
2. Replace repeated trap scans with point-indexed lookup.
3. Make material reactions source/event-driven and index ground items.
4. Cache item proc topology and per-tick derived stats.
5. Then profile browser rendering separately.

content.text:
Yes. **Town planning is the biggest startup bottleneck I found.** In a headless probe of the default overworld start, planning took about **4 seconds** on seed `0xC0FFEE`, while placing the planned chunks and entities took another **117–147 ms**. The slowest part was surveying town and resource sites. Nearby candidates repeatedly scan much of the same terrain. Precomputing terrain counts and nearest-feature distances could preserve the existing scores, tie-breaking, and seeded layouts while removing those repeated scans. [Town placement](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/environment/dungeon/townPlacement.js:327)

Two other opportunities depend on what feels slow:

- **Begin → first visible frame.** The default start schedules 137 animation-frame waits across world planning, chunk placement, and the opening map bake. That’s roughly 2.3 seconds of frame intervals at 60 Hz, though actual wall time depends on how the work fits into those frames. Yielding when a time budget runs out would let cheap batches run together while keeping the loading panel responsive. [World generation](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/environment/dungeon/index.js:78) · [Opening map bake](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/display/camera/openingLandscape.js:10)
- **First visible frame → player control.** The opening flyover alone has a minimum of **8.2 seconds** of travel, plus landmark holds and a short blend. A skip control would give players the largest immediate improvement in time to play. Yes. **The combat HUD is the best next target.** It recalculates combat stats, expected weapon damage, status rows, and ammo on every animation frame, even while the player is idle. In a seeded headless probe, that one update averaged **2.17 ms per call**, with a **2.57 ms p95**. Refreshing it after a rules turn or an explicit HUD invalidation could recover most of that time between turns. Same-turn changes such as equipment swaps and debug commands need an invalidation path. [Combat HUD](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/main/ui/hudFeeds.js:458) · [Frame loop](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/main.js:6230)

Two more candidates:

- **Engine: reuse one status snapshot per actor during intent validation.** The system can build three snapshots to check stasis, action lock, and immobilization. An in-memory prototype dropped the isolated pass from **0.248 to 0.129 ms** on the same seeded world. This is a small change with a clear regression target: preserve the current ordering and cancellation behavior. [Intent validation](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/systems/intentValidationSystem.js:134)
- **Rendering: classify roofs once per tile per frame.** Overworld lighting can query the same roof up to 64 times while applying ambient light, then again while computing darkness. Both passes could read the same tile mask. I verified the repeated lookups in code. The savings still need a benchmark. [Lighting engine](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/display/lighting/engine.js:982)
